content.title: Home again! Artemis II crew splashes down safely in the Pacific
content.text: 10:05 pm ET April 10, 2026Video of Artemis II astronauts exiting OrionBrooke EdwardsMiss the action? Check out this video recap of the astronauts exiting the spacecraft after their journey around the moon.10:01 pm ET April 10, 2026Astronauts taken to waiting shipBrooke EdwardsThe four astronauts have been taken via helicopter to an awaiting recovery ship, ending their journey back from the moon.9:54 pm ET April 10, 2026'Path to the surface is open'Brooke EdwardsNASA Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya says that while there is work to be done to assess how Integrity, the Orion spacecraft, performed during the mission, he is confident that progress toward the future Artemis missions has been made.“I think the path to the surface is open now,” said Kshatriya. “This was an incredible test of an incredible machine.”9:35 pm ET April 10, 2026Astronauts out of OrionBrooke EdwardsAll crew members are out of the Orion spacecraft. They will be flown one at a time to the awaiting ship.9:28 pm ET April 10, 2026Astronauts about to exit spacecraftBrooke EdwardsThe crew will soon exit the spacecraft. Two helicopters will alternate as they pick up the four astronauts one at a time.9:23 pm ET April 10, 2026Congressman Haridopolos remarks on Artemis IIBrooke EdwardsFlorida Congressman Mike Haridopolos spoke with Fox News’ Jesse Watters Primetime following the splashdown.“It’s incredible −10 days in space, farther than any astronauts have ever traveled. And it all started at Kennedy Space Center in my district, where the country came together to watch history,” Congressman Haridopolos is quoted. “We are making historic investments in NASA because America is back, and as NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman just texted me, ‘we’re just getting started.’” 9:15 pm ET April 10, 2026All astronauts doing wellBrooke EdwardsThe navy divers report all four astronauts are doing well and happy to be home.9:13 pm ET April 10, 2026Navy divers in OrionBrooke EdwardsFour navy divers with medical training are in the spacecraft checking out the astronauts before the "front porch" is deployed. The stabilization collar is currently being installed − which will help keep the spacecraft from too much movement in the water.The crew reported doing well, but caution is being exercised.8:57 pm ET April 10, 2026Crowd reacts to Artemis II splashdownBrooke EdwardsCheck out this video of an Artemis II watch party in San Diego.8:57 pm ET April 10, 2026Orion side hatch opened!Brooke EdwardsNext the recovery teams will set up the "front porch".8:33 pm ET April 10, 2026NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman on shipBrooke EdwardsNASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is onboard the recovery ship and just gave his thoughts.“I’m still at a loss for words,” said Isaacman. “The childhood Jared right now can’t believe what I just saw. I’ve almost been waiting my whole lifetime to see this, and as NASA Administrator I just couldn’t be more proud of the entire workforce.""The years, the effort, the late nights, all the hard work from across the country that contributed to this incredible moment right now," said Isaacman.8:23 pm ET April 10, 2026Recovery teams closing inBrooke EdwardsThe recovery teams are approaching the Orion spacecraft. Next up, the "front porch" will be deployed.The crew and Mission Control are working on communication issues leading into the arrival of the recovery teams.8:13 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II crew safe and wellBrooke Edwards"What a journey!" said Commander Reid Wiseman to Mission Control. "Four green crew members."Green meaning "doing well".8:08 pm ET April 10, 2026Splashdown! Artemis II is home!Brooke EdwardsThe Artemis II Orion spacecraft is safely in the Pacific Ocean. Recovery crews will soon make their way to the astronauts once safe to do so.8:05 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II parachutes deployed!Brooke EdwardsAll parachutes have successfully been deployed! Next up is a 20 mph splashdown in the Pacific Ocean.7:53 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II spacecraft begins reentryBrooke EdwardsAs they race back through the atmosphere, the astronauts will experience a six-minute communications blackout period. This is expected as the plasma outside the spacecraft blocks the communication signals.The crew will experience upwards of 3.9 Gs. To the astronauts it will feel like 3.9 times the force of gravity pushing them into their seats.Once Orion reaches between 35,000 and 24,000 feet above the sea, the forward bay cover will jettison for parachute release.7:44 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II headed for splashdownBrooke EdwardsOrion is descending at a rate of 15,000 feet per second.The upcoming pyrotechnic events during reentry, such as the parachutes deploying, will be a rough yet welcomed experience for the astronauts.“They’re going to hear. They’re going to feel them,” said Artemis II Lead Flight Director Jeff Radigan during the April 9 press briefing. “It’s actually, I think going to be a fun ride for them.”The astronauts are looking out for hearing and feeling these sensations as it signifies all is proceeding well during their ride down to Earth inside Orion.7:38 pm ET April 10, 2026Raise burn completeBrooke EdwardsThe Orion spacecraft completed one last adjustment to ensure a successful reentry. This is a 19-second firing of the spacecraft's thrusters.7:34 pm ET April 10, 2026Orion service module jettisonedBrooke EdwardsNASA has reported that the Orion spacecraft has separated from its crew module – the bottom part of the spacecraft which stores thrusters, power, and life support.This is necessary, as it exposes the spacecraft’s heatshield. The heatshield will take the brunt of the friction and heat during reentry.Not to worry, as the service module is no longer needed.7:24 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II splashdown, return to EarthBrooke EdwardsHere's a look at the journey Orion will soon be taking as the Artemis II crew returns to Earth.7:14 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II splashdown in less than an hourBrooke EdwardsSplashdown is quickly approaching. The next milestone is set for 7:33 p.m. when the Orion spacecraft and service module separate.7:03 pm ET April 10, 2026NASA astronaut posts photo as Artemis II heads homeBrooke EdwardsNASA astronaut, Jessica Meir, posted this colorful view from the International Space Station.6:55 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II zero-g indicatorBrooke EdwardsRise, the Artemis II zero-g indicator, has been an entertaining feature during the entire mission, even taking over NASA's social media page for a day.Rise also carried a microSD card with the names of all members of the public who submitted their names to fly on the Artemis II mission.Rise was created by a second-grade student in California and was selected out of submissions from more than 50 countries. The design was inspired by the iconic "Earthrise" photo taken by the Apollo 8 crew from lunar orbit.6:42 pm ET April 10, 2026How fast will the Artemis II crew go?Brooke EdwardsThe Artemis II crew has a fast commute home! When blazing through the atmosphere, they will be traveling at a max speed of 24,661 mph − or 33 times the speed of sound.The Artemis II crew will end that commute with a splashdown at a slow 19 mph.6:35 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II crew suited up and readyBrooke EdwardsThe Artemis II crew is suited, seated and ready for the upcoming splashdown. They are around 12,000 miles out.6:31 pm ET April 10, 2026NASA live ahead of Artemis II splashdownBrooke EdwardsNASA is live ahead of the upcoming return of Artemis II. The video is posted above, below the countdown clock.6:26 pm ET April 10, 2026Beyond Artemis IIBrooke EdwardsAstronauts have not left low Earth orbit since the Apollo 17 mission in 1972. Now that Artemis II has broke that exploration pause − and set a new space travel distance record − NASA vows this is only the beginning.The core stage of the Artemis III SLS rocket is set to travel to Kennedy Space Center as soon as late this month. Artemis III will see the Orion spacecraft dock with either a SpaceX or Blue Origin lunar lander in low Earth orbit. Set for 2027, this mission will pave the way for a moon landing with the Artemis IV mission.That return to the moon could happen as soon as 2028.Going beyond the return to the moon, NASA has plans for a moon base − setting the stage for a permanent presence and eventual journey to Mars.6:15 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II moon photosBrooke EdwardsHere's another look at the stunning photos taken by the Artemis II astronauts during their flight around the moon. During the trip, the crew saw features of the moon never seen by human eyes − plus a solar eclipse as the moon blocked the sun from their perspective!Just how breathtaking were these views in person? The astronauts were heard on multiple occasions having trouble putting into words what they were witnessing.6:09 pm ET April 10, 2026Haridopolos asks Artemis II astronauts questionBrooke Edwards and Rick NealeEarlier this week, U.S. Rep. Mike Haridopolos fielded potential questions from his constituents to ask the Artemis II astronauts. During a live call Thursday, April 9, the Indian Harbour Beach Republican asked the crew a question submitted by Renee of Indian River County:“What were you thinking when you were going around the moon − the furthest ever from Earth on the dark side of the moon?”Pilot Victor Glover replied that the astronauts were busy working on science, and he took a brief moment to say a short prayer of gratitude for being sent on this mission.“I was hoping that people looked up and were watching to see when we came back into communication. And that maybe there was a chance that folks would feel a sense of togetherness,” Glover said.5:57 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II splashdown in just over 2 hoursBrooke EdwardsThe astronauts are currently heading home to Earth after traveling 690,000 miles around the moon and back. They will splashdown off the coast of San Diego. NASA states the return will be too far out for those on land to view, but also urges all boaters to stay clear of the recovery area.3:38 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II approaching EarthBrooke EdwardsThe Artemis II astronauts are getting closer to home. As of around 3:30 p.m., they are less than 35,000 miles out.12:26 pm ET April 10, 2026Artemis II astronauts awakeBrooke EdwardsNASA has posted that the Artemis II crew is awake ahead of the eventful day ahead. They will soon begin to prepare for the trip down to Earth.Their wake up song? "Run to the Water" by Live.10:53 am ET April 10, 2026Artemis II splashdown tonightBrooke EdwardsSplashdown is set for 8:07 p.m. EDT. in the Pacific Ocean, off the coast of San Diego.FLORIDA TODAY will have continuous live updates leading into the reentry of the Orion spacecraft, beginning at 6 p.m.
